claim: Google's revenue-share payment to Apple in 2022 was an estimated $20 billion, as found by the D.C. District Court in the underlying liability opinion and reaffirmed in the September 2025 remedies opinion.
stance_target: quantifying Google TAC/search-placement revenue as an estimation-method figure given Apple's own filings never disclose it
scope_conditions: United States v. Google LLC, No. 1:20-cv-03010-APM, court-surfaced trial finding, calendar year 2022
quoted_support: Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars. Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d at 90 ¶ 299 (finding that Google's revenue share payment to Apple in 2022 was an estimated $20 billion).
numbers: $20 billion estimated 2022 Google-to-Apple revenue share payment

claim: Google's total 2021 'traffic acquisition costs' paid to all distribution partners (not just Apple) exceeded $26 billion, per the court's liability-phase factual finding, and the court noted that figure 'has likely grown since.'
stance_target: total TAC pool size as an upper bound context for the Apple-specific $20B figure
scope_conditions: United States v. Google LLC liability findings, calendar year 2021, all distribution partners combined
quoted_support: In 2021, Google paid more than $26 billion in 'traffic acquisition costs' to distribution partners. Google, 747 F. Supp. 3d at 88-89 ¶ 289. That number has likely grown since.
numbers: $26 billion total 2021 Google traffic acquisition costs, all partners

claim: The court explicitly rejected a full payment ban on Google's search-distribution revenue-share payments, reasoning that on 'day one' post-judgment distributors including Apple would keep Google as default anyway (because it is the best product), so a ban would strip payments without shifting competition and would hand Google 'a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars.'
stance_target: the near-term risk that a court remedy eliminates the Google TAC arrangement entirely
scope_conditions: Remedies phase, United States v. Google LLC, decided September 2, 2025
quoted_support: Though the bases for a payment ban are sound, the court declines to impose such a remedy at this time... Freed of having to pay billions in revenue share, Google's profits would increase. Not paying Apple alone would result in a windfall worth tens of billions of dollars.
numbers: tens of billions of dollars windfall to Google if payment ban imposed

claim: The remedy actually ordered requires Google's distribution agreements to be non-exclusive and lets OEMs/carriers switch default search providers on a one-year option, but permits Google to CONTINUE paying for default placement -- the payment stream itself is not banned, only its exclusivity.
stance_target: the assumption that any adverse Google antitrust ruling terminates Apple's TAC revenue
scope_conditions: Final remedy design, United States v. Google LLC, September 2025 memorandum opinion
quoted_support: So, for now, Google will be permitted to pay distributors for default placement. There are strong reasons not to jolt the system and to allow market forces to do the work... The court is thus prepared to revisit a payment ban (or a lesser remedy) if competition is not substantially restored through the remedies the court does impose.
time_period: ongoing, judgment term begins 60 days after entry

claim: The court modified the final judgment to explicitly prohibit Google from entering an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product (e.g., Gemini) in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device -- Apple is named specifically in this provision.
stance_target: the remedy extends beyond legacy search-default exclusivity to future GenAI product distribution exclusivity involving Apple specifically
scope_conditions: Section III.L modification, United States v. Google LLC final judgment
quoted_support: And to leave no doubt that Apple falls within the revision, Section III.L of Google's RPFJ shall be modified to make clear that Google is prohibited from entering into an exclusive agreement with Apple to distribute any Google GenAI product either in any Safari mode or on any Apple mobile or desktop device.

claim: The final judgment's term is six years total (a five-year decree plus one year to build compliance infrastructure and the Technical Committee), taking effect 60 days after entry, with the parties ordered to submit a revised joint final judgment by September 10, 2025 -- giving a concrete timetable for how long the current, largely-preserved payment arrangement runs before the judgment could next be revisited.
stance_target: remedy timetable is analysable and falls within or just past the report's 2-5 year holding window
scope_conditions: United States v. Google LLC, final judgment terms
quoted_support: For that reason, the court believes that a five-year term, plus an additional one year to put the infrastructure and processes in place to implement the remedies, is appropriate... As to the effective date, the final judgment shall take effect 60 days after it is entered.
numbers: September 10, 2025 deadline for revised joint final judgment

claim: Apple SVP of Services Eddy Cue testified during the remedies phase that GenAI represents, for the first time in over a decade, a genuine opportunity to challenge Google's search dominance by 'taking LLMs and search indexes and combining those two things,' a statement the court cited when deciding to shorten the judgment term from the DOJ's proposed 10 years to 5-6 years.
stance_target: late-follower AI strategy question -- Apple's own executive frames GenAI as a structural opening rather than a threat requiring an arms race
scope_conditions: remedies-phase trial testimony, United States v. Google LLC, 2025
quoted_support: [F]or the first time, I think there's an opportunity [to challenge Google] because there's new technology... we're seeing some real... investment by taking LLMs and search indexes and combining those two things to provide what I think is potentially a better experience.

claim: The court found Google's high revenue-share payments 'disincentivize Apple from launching its own search engine,' with Apple's Eddy Cue not disputing that the payments were 'a significant amount of money' and a disincentive, even as Cue maintained Apple was unlikely to enter search regardless because 'Google does an amazing job.'
stance_target: the Google TAC arrangement functions as a structural incentive against Apple building competing search/AI capability, bearing on whether late-follower status is a deliberate strategic choice or a rent-seeking equilibrium
scope_conditions: remedies-phase testimony, United States v. Google LLC
quoted_support: The court found that '[t]he prospect of losing tens of billions in guaranteed revenue from Google—which presently come at little to no cost to Apple—disincentivizes Apple from launching its own search engine when it otherwise has built the capacity to do so.' ... Cue added that Apple still was unlikely to enter the search business because 'Google does an amazing job.'
time_period: 2025 remedies-phase testimony; underlying finding from August 2024 liability opinion
